papers.title: State-space symmetry in Boolean network ensembles
papers.abstract: Studies of evolving Boolean network systems have found that Boolean functions cluster into equivalence classes with a characteristic frequency distribution - a pattern governed by the Zyklenzeiger symmetry group - but the dynamical origin of this symmetry has remained unexplained. Here we show that it is a consequence of a fundamental symmetry of Boolean network dynamics itself. A Boolean network consists of nodes that update according to Boolean functions of their regulatory inputs; its global dynamics is encoded in a state-space network. We identify the dynamical symmetry group of ensembles of Boolean networks that average over random interaction topologies: for networks with $N$ nodes, it is the $N$-dimensional hyperoctahedral group, generated by node-flips and node-label permutations. These transformations are admissible for every Boolean network regardless of topology; for random-topology ensembles, including all ensembles of fixed in-degree $K<N$, they constitute the complete symmetry group. We also show that input-label permutations constitute a hidden gauge freedom of the dynamics. The Zyklenzeiger symmetry of Boolean functions follows directly from the node-flips of the hyperoctahedral group together with this gauge freedom. Boolean networks related by the hyperoctahedral group have isomorphic state-space networks and form its orbits, and Burnside's lemma gives the number of these orbits for any fixed network topology. It provides a symmetry reduction of the analysis of Boolean network dynamics and explains why the Boolean functions of evolved networks fall into Zyklenzeiger classes, and why these classes split in finite networks.

papers.title: From the possible to the optimal: differentiable optimization of gene regulatory networks
papers.abstract: Understanding the space of ``the actual and the possible'' regulatory architectures capable of realizing biological functions is one of the major challenges in biology. Optimization-based approaches can rationalize regulatory mechanisms from functional objectives and constraints, but their computational cost has limited them to finding individual solutions. Here, we introduce \texttt{jaxgrn}, a framework that combines differentiable programming with stochastic simulations of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) to optimize thousands of networks end-to-end on GPUs. Using morphogen-driven embryonic patterning as a case study, we optimize networks for domain formation and positional information, while varying constraints on input noise, boundary precision and scaling with system size. While recovering known archetypes for scaling, we find that varying the constraints organizes optimal solutions into qualitatively distinct regimes. When optimizing domain formation, we observe phenotypic convergence across a continuum of regulatory architectures, ranging from input-driven to feedback-driven networks. When optimizing positional information, solutions are initially phenotypically diverse despite moderate variation in regulatory architecture; imposing scaling drives both phenotypic and regulatory convergence of the optimized networks onto a few recurring regulatory architectures. Our systematic approach opens the door for variational systems biology in which changing functional constraints reshape the landscape of possible phenotypes and regulatory architectures.

papers.title: A Structural Theory of Admissible Transitions in Biological Reaction Networks
papers.abstract: Biological reaction networks exhibit transient changes that cannot be understood from steady states or long-term persistence alone. We extend Chemical Organization Theory to transitions between species subsets, using stoichiometry and feasible reaction fluxes to characterize structurally admissible changes without specifying kinetic parameters. The framework distinguishes algebraic admissibility from feasibility constrained by reactant availability. We relate these transitions to reaction-based ordinary differential equations and identify an asymmetry: closure-building transitions are determined by network structure, whereas subsequent reductions can depend on the realized trajectory. Transitions to terminal organizations are characterized when the relevant species sets occur along that trajectory. An HIV-immune response model illustrates how a shared closure-building phase can precede different long-term outcomes. The framework connects continuous dynamics with discrete changes in species composition and supports structural analysis of transient pathways and organization formation in systems biology, while distinguishing structural admissibility from realization under particular kinetics.
